stories.headline: Update: San Juan River crests at second-highest level on record in Pagosa Springs, short of 1911 mark
stories.summary:
The San Juan River in Pagosa Springs crested at 16.81 feet Sunday night, the second-highest level on record. It fell short of the 22-foot crest forecasters had feared and the 1911 record. Preliminary National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration gauge data show the crest was nearly two feet higher than the Oct. 23 flood peak and still constitutes major flooding.

An estimated 3 to 4 inches of rain fell on ground already saturated by the earlier storm, with reservoirs near capacity. National Weather Service meteorologist Eric Petersen said the water had nowhere to go. Meteorologist Lucas Boyer of the Grand Junction office said the deepest moisture has passed but flood impacts will continue as runoff from smaller creeks feeds larger rivers.

Mandatory evacuations were ordered in parts of La Plata, Archuleta, Rio Grande, Mineral, Conejos and Montezuma counties, including parts of Pagosa Springs, Durango, Del Norte, Ignacio and Mancos. In Archuleta County, all low-lying areas along the San Juan, Rio Blanco, Navajo and Piedra rivers are under orders, and the rest of the county was asked to shelter in place.

Widespread road and highway closures remain in effect, and law enforcement urged residents to avoid all non-essential travel. Pagosa Springs residents had only just been allowed to return home from the previous week's evacuation when the new orders were announced.

stories.headline: Denver transportation chief Amy Ford steps down amid City Council criticism
stories.summary:
Amy Ford, who has led Denver's Department of Transportation & Infrastructure since December 2023, is leaving to pursue another opportunity, Mayor Mike Johnston announced Monday. Her departure comes amid growing City Council criticism of the agency's spending and operations.

Johnston credited Ford with delivering complex projects on time and on budget. Her tenure included completion of Colfax Bus Rapid Transit, investments in Safe Routes to School, Vision Zero measures to reduce traffic deaths and the new High Line Canal Trail pedestrian and bike underpass.

Council criticism has focused on the trash program, which collects about $33 million in service charges but costs about $42.9 million to operate, not counting fleet costs. Monthly rates range from $9 to $21 depending on cart size. The department is slated to receive a $6 million general fund subsidy for the program next year, and Ford has said a rate study and likely price increase will be needed.

In September budget hearings, Ford also faced criticism over a decision to require solid waste employees to work on holidays including Martin Luther King Jr. Day, Sí se Puede Day, Juneteenth and Indigenous Peoples Day. Councilmember Amanda Sandoval called the policy unacceptable.

stories.headline: Kadri, Schwartz each score twice as Avalanche beat Blackhawks 5-2
stories.summary:
Nazem Kadri and Jaden Schwartz each scored two goals Monday night as the Colorado Avalanche snapped a three-game road losing streak with a 5-2 win over Chicago at United Center. T.J. Hughes recorded his first multi-point game with two assists, and Mackenzie Blackwood made 21 saves. The Avalanche have won three straight.

Colorado fell behind 2-0 in the first seven minutes. Wyatt Kaiser scored 57 seconds in on a puck that deflected off Cale Makar, and Roman Kantserov added a goal off a 2-on-1 created by Connor Bedard. A Martin Necas goal was waved off after Chicago successfully challenged for goalie interference.

Kadri gave Colorado its first lead with a power-play goal at 13:38 of the second period, the team's fifth try with the extra man, after Makar's shot from the top of the zone. It was his fourth goal of the season, all in the past five games. Schwartz added his sixth of the year with 10.6 seconds left in the period, deflecting a Sam Malinski shot past goalie Spencer Knight.

Coach Jared Bednar called the start sleepy but said the team responded quickly once its urgency rose.

stories.headline: Young Colorado voters look beyond party lines, feel left behind, experts say
stories.summary:
More than one-third of Coloradans are between 18 and 34, making young adults one of the state's most influential voting blocs. Experts say many feel disconnected from the political establishment and unconvinced that elected officials understand their economic pressures, particularly housing affordability, student debt and career opportunities.

Phil Chen, an associate professor of political science at the University of Denver, called young people the most economically precarious age group. He said many doubt they will be able to buy a home or rely on Social Security.

Janet Donavan, a teaching professor at the University of Colorado's political science department, said young voters are looking for different answers. While young Coloradans are more likely to identify as Democrats than Republicans, most are unaffiliated, echoing the statewide trend. Donavan said older generations typically joined a party and drifted away over time, while Gen Z and younger millennials are bypassing parties from the start.

Representation is also a factor. The average U.S. representative is 57 and the average senator is 64. In the Colorado General Assembly, the average state representative is just under 49 and the average senator just under 54. The two youngest legislators, Rep. Dusty Johnson and Sen. Katie Wallace, were both born in 1995.

stories.headline: U.S. Treasury approves all 91 Colorado Opportunity Zones
stories.summary:
The U.S. Treasury has approved all 91 areas Colorado nominated as federally designated Opportunity Zones in the program's second round, the state announced Monday. The number is the maximum the state could submit. The zones go live for investment on Jan. 1.

The program offers investors tax benefits for long-term investments in real estate, infrastructure and operating businesses in designated low-income communities. Gov. Jared Polis estimated the new zones could draw more than $4 billion in investment statewide.

Thirty-nine zones are in Denver, Adams, Arapahoe and Jefferson counties, including every eligible neighborhood on Denver's Mile High Line, Sun Valley and Globeville. Eight are in El Paso County, including the North Nevada Corridor and Printers Hill.

The state submitted the zones in September after a monthslong stakeholder process led by the Office of Economic Development & International Trade. Leaders prioritized rural areas and regions outside the Front Range. The office will provide grant funding to communities within the zones to help attract investment, with guidance on the grants to be released later.

stories.headline: Downtown Denver Development Authority approves $3.5 million for Mile High Innovation Program
stories.summary:
Denver's Downtown Development Authority has approved up to $3.5 million to fund a private operator for the city's new Mile High Innovation Program, aimed at drawing startups into the central business district. The operator will work under Denver Economic Development & Opportunity and will be chosen through competitive procurement, with no timetable set.

The funding comes as Upper Downtown faces office vacancies reported at 46% or higher. Some tenants have moved to LoDo, RiNo and Cherry Creek, and others have left Colorado. The money is drawn from the authority's $40 million Open Denver program, which relies on tax increment financing. The economic development agency previously announced $1.5 million in additional operating support, bringing total operating funds to $5 million.

The program will center on a 30,000-square-foot innovation and entrepreneurship hub in Independence Plaza, developed with the University of Colorado Denver. The university bought the building at 17th and Arapahoe streets in August for a reported $28 million. The tower once sold for more than $120 million and is reportedly over 75% vacant.

Open Denver is part of a broader $100 million Denver Jobs Agenda aimed at generating 10,000 jobs citywide.

stories.headline: Eats on the Platte food hall opens in Denver's Sun Valley neighborhood
stories.summary:
Eats on the Platte, an 8,000-square-foot food hall at 2500 W. 10th Ave., opened Friday in Denver's Sun Valley neighborhood. It launched with five local vendors: Wings Social Co., Jama Miami Cuban, Jalapeño Business, La Brewjula Café and Corazón de Tita. More vendors are expected in 2027.

The Denver Housing Authority is leading broader redevelopment of Sun Valley, a historically diverse neighborhood once known as The Bottoms. About 94% of residents live in subsidized housing and more than 80% live below the poverty line. The effort includes new housing, better neighborhood connections and expanded access to food and parks.

The hall sits near the site of an 11-acre Riverfront Park along the South Platte River. Construction on the first phase began Oct. 21, and the park is expected to open in late 2027.

The hall is operated with Kitchen Network, Denver's largest and longest-running commissary kitchen, which supports about 100 specialty food businesses a year. Vendors get access to professional kitchen infrastructure and business support. It is open 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. Sunday through Thursday and 9 a.m. to 11 p.m. Friday and Saturday.

stories.headline: Two Denver Pavilions restaurants temporarily close as new steakhouse opens in Aurora
stories.summary:
Two restaurants at the Denver Pavilions are closed, at least temporarily. 5280 Burger Bar off Glenarm Place has been shut for several weeks for repairs and renovation, according to a sign on the door. Maggiano's Little Italy posted a sign saying it is closed for maintenance.

A Denver Pavilions spokesperson said the closures are not due to a larger infrastructure problem and called the timing unfortunate and coincidental. Maggiano's could reopen as soon as this week, while 5280 Burger Bar's reopening may be delayed by a complicated HVAC repair.

Elsewhere, a new steakhouse called Savor has opened at Arapahoe Crossing, 6676 S. Parker Road in Aurora, in a former Old Chicago location. Executive Chef Muthu Pandy's menu includes starters, flatbreads, steaks, pastas and desserts made in-house. The restaurant is open 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. Tuesday through Sunday, with the bar open until 10 p.m., and can host private events for up to 42 people.

The column also noted the opening of Eats on the Platte, a food hall operated by the Denver Housing Authority at 2500 W. 10th Ave.

stories.headline: Denver tiny home community La Paz switches to substance-free model
stories.summary:
The La Paz tiny home village for people experiencing homelessness, at 2301 S. Santa Fe Drive in Denver's Overland neighborhood, began transitioning to a substance-free model Nov. 1, according to the Denver Department of Housing Stability. The change is expected to be complete by early next year.

The Colorado Village Collaborative and the city run the shelter, which opened in March 2024 as part of Mayor Mike Johnston's All in Mile High effort. CEO Jessica Ehinger said La Paz will become a self-selective community in which all members have volunteered for substance-free living. Applicants must sign an agreement outlining expectations before joining the waitlist, and the community will have an exit policy.

Residents who do not want to take part will be sent to the Steele community or other city-run shelters with lower barriers. The Steele village will remain a low-barrier shelter with intake through city outreach teams. Both sites still prohibit active drug use or dealing on the property.

A 2022 zoning standard limits tiny home sites to four-year spans. The first village, Monroe, expired in September. La Paz and Steele permits run until 2028 and 2029, respectively.

stories.headline: Free and cheap things to do around Denver in November
stories.summary:
Golden Gate Canyon State Park will host a Christmas Tree Cut on Dec. 5, offering 250 permits through a lottery. Applications are open online through Nov. 15 at cpwshop.com, and permits cost $35 per tree with a limit of one per household. A random drawing is set for the 16th, and winners can cut a tree from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. A Colorado State Park pass is required for each vehicle.

Hudson Holidays returns to The Hudson Gardens & Event Center in Littleton from Nov. 27 to Jan. 3, 2027. It features more than 200 wrapped trees, 10 themed areas, a 9,000-square-foot light maze and an animated light show. Any Day tickets are $25 for adults, $23 for seniors and $20 for youth, with a presale special Nov. 6 to 8 at $15 for adults and seniors and $10 for youth.

Good Times is giving away a free scoop of frozen custard every Friday in November, on the 6th, 13th, 20th and 27th, at in-restaurant locations.

The Celebrate Shop, a marketplace for entrepreneurs with disabilities, will be held at The Curtis Hotel on Nov. 6 and 7, with free parking in the hotel garage.

topStory.headline: US Midterm Elections Held Amid Iran Conflict, Record Federal Monitoring and Narrow Congressional Margins
topStory.summary:
Americans voted Tuesday in midterm elections that will determine control of Congress for the final two years of President Donald Trump's second term. All 435 House seats are on the ballot, along with 35 Senate seats (33 regular contests and special elections in Florida and Ohio), 39 governorships and thousands of state and local offices and ballot measures on taxes, abortion rights and voting rules. Republicans hold a narrow House majority, and Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control. In the Senate, Republicans hold 53 seats to 47 for Democrats and their independent allies, and Democrats also need a net gain of four seats for a majority.

History favors the opposition party: the president's party has lost House seats in 18 of the past 20 midterm elections, a 90 percent rate dating to 1946. Trump faces falling poll numbers and pressure from within the Republican Party to end the war with Iran, which began in February when the US and Israel attacked the country. In Michigan's Senate race, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed held a final rally after Rep. Haley Stevens endorsed Republican Mike Rogers, an unexpected development a day earlier.

The administration's election-related actions drew attention on the eve of voting. The Supreme Court rejected the president's effort to target alleged noncitizen voters, a defeat for the administration. The Justice Department said it would send roughly 1,000 election monitors to polling places in all 50 states, compared with 289 in the 2022 midterms and 714 in the 2024 presidential election. Harmeet Dhillon, head of the department's Civil Rights Division, said monitors would also seek to ensure votes were not canceled out by someone who "shouldn't be voting." Federal monitors have been used by both parties' administrations, though Texas, Florida and Missouri tried in 2024 to block Biden administration monitors.

The Iran conflict overlapped with the election. US officials told CBS and NBC that the military carried out limited, defensive strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, in response to Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps fire on a US aircraft and ongoing attempts to target shipping and US assets. Iranian state media reported explosions on Qeshm, and the IRGC said it shot down two US MQM-170 drones and a US MQ-9 drone. Officials said the strikes were not a resumption of major combat operations, and the US military did not comment.

Trump said he was in "no rush" to escalate, telling Axios the US had "crippled them financially," though he told Fox News the US might need to target an underground nuclear-linked site known as Pickaxe Mountain. He denied that major strikes would resume after the election, but the Associated Press, citing two regional officials, reported that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu urged him in a weekend call to authorize another wave. Iran's chief negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said "the ball is now in America's court to prevent war," and Qatar said both sides were reviewing mediators' proposals. Iranian negotiators had reportedly discussed reopening the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the US met seven conditions, including lifting a naval blockade.
